We conjecture that a refined concept of a simple solution might yield an approximation factor of 4. 5 Conclusion We have introduced permissive vertex splitting, which generalizes the earlier exclusive and inclusive vertex splitting notions by allowing symmetry with respect to “positive” and “negative” pairwise similarity data. Our type of vertex splitting turns out to be quite satisfying, as it corresponds to a natural definition of overlapping clustering. Unfortunately, the general case of Correlation Clustering with Permissive Vertex Splitting is rather intractable, as it is para-NP-hard and admits no n1−ε approximation in polynomial time for any ε > 0 (unless P = NP). On the positive side, when restricted to datasets with complete data we obtain a kernel with O(k 3 ) vertices and a polynomial time 7-approximation. Interesting questions remain, for example whether one can reduce our approximation factor to 4 (or even lower), whether a kernel with only linearly many vertices exists (as is the case when only inclusive splits and edge-edits are allowed [1]), or whether refined lower bounds in terms of running time or approximation factor can be found. Future work might also consider the parameterized complexity of Correlation Clustering with Permissive Vertex Splitting and Cluster Editing with Permissive Vertex Splitting with respect to structural parameters of the input, or with restrictions on the number of clusters which contain any given node.
